title: Noor and the Witness
premise: Ansel Okonkwo, a meticulous estate lawyer in the fading town of Harrow Bend, is reading a will for a dead man when twin letters arrive at his office: one confessing to a murder the town buried three years ago, the other promising a fuller confession if Ansel can identify the writer before the statute of limitations expires. The dead testator, it turns out, witnessed the killing and hid the proof inside his own estate documents, making Ansel the unwitting custodian of the truth. As Ansel and Noor Haddad, the victim's sister who arrives posing as a paralegal, decode the file, they realize the killer is someone who has had access to every legal record in town. In the end, Ansel baits the killer with a forged codicil naming a fictional beneficiary, forcing a confession he records, and chooses to hand the evidence to the victim's family first, letting justice arrive outside the courtroom before the law can claim it.
about_author: Wendell Whitlock spent a decade as a probate clerk in small-town Ohio before turning to fiction, a career that left him with an archivist's love of paper trails and a skeptic's view of official justice. He writes mysteries about people who keep secrets for a living, and lives quietly where the county records room still smells of toner and dust.

chapters.title: The Will That Wasn't Filed
chapters.summary: Ansel Okonkwo's POV. Ansel reads the will of Elias Grange, a hoarder who died with no known heirs, and finds a codicil referencing a document that doesn't exist in any registry. A letter slips from the file: a confession to the drowning of Danny Haddad three years ago, ruled an accident. The beat: unease — Ansel's ordered world develops a crack.

chapters.title: Second Letter, Same Hand
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. A second letter arrives, promising the full truth if Ansel can name the writer before the statute expires in six weeks. The handwriting matches the first. Sheriff's Deputy Colm Reyes, an old friend, mentions the Haddad case was closed too neatly. The beat: dread mixed with the first thrill of a puzzle worth solving.

chapters.title: The Paralegal Who Knew Too Much
chapters.summary: Noor Haddad's POV. A capable temp named Noor joins the firm, asking precise questions about the Grange estate. Ansel catches her photographing the codicil and confronts her; she reveals she is Danny's sister, convinced he was murdered and that Elias Grange saw it happen. The beat: wary alliance — two people with different reasons to want the same truth.

chapters.title: Inventory of a Hoarder
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Ansel and Noor catalog Grange's house, finding his obsessive habit of documenting everything — receipts, dates, photographs of the river on the night Danny died. One photo shows a second figure on the bank, face turned away. The beat: mounting excitement curdling into fear as they realize the killer may know what Grange kept.

chapters.title: Everyone Who Touched the File
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel audits who accessed the Haddad case records: the deputy who closed it, the coroner, the town clerk, and — uncomfortably — his own predecessor at the firm. Someone has been in his office; a folder is re-shelved wrong by millimeters. The beat: paranoia — the file cabinet becomes a crime scene.

chapters.title: The Confession That Doesn't Fit
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Noor tests the confession's details against what she knows of Danny's last night and finds one deliberate error — the killer wrote a detail only the police report contained, not the riverbank. The writer is someone who read the file but wasn't there. The beat: the trap inverts; the letters are a game played by someone watching them play it.

chapters.title: Clerk of Secrets
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel traces the typewriter font to the county records room and confronts the town clerk, Marla Voss, who kept duplicate copies of every case for 'personal archives.' Marla admits selling quiet erasures for years — including edits to the Haddad file — but swears she isn't the letter writer. The beat: the machinery of buried justice exposed, and a new suspect list.

chapters.title: What the Predecessor Kept
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. In the firm's dead storage, Noor finds Ansel's predecessor's private notes: he discovered the Haddad cover-up, blackmailed the killer, and died conveniently of a heart attack a year ago. The killer has been inside the firm's history all along — and the letters were a test of whether Ansel would dig. The beat: grief and fury; the case was never cold, just curated.

chapters.title: The Forged Codicil
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Ansel drafts a fake codicil 'discovering' Grange's hidden photograph, names a fictional beneficiary, and schedules a public reading, betting the killer must destroy it before witnesses. Noor watches the records room; the deputy watches the office. The beat: coiled suspense — the hunters become bait, and everyone knows the clock is running out.

chapters.title: Statute of Limitations
chapters.summary: Ansel and Noor's POV, interleaved. At the reading, the coroner — the man who signed the false report and wrote the letters to relive his control — comes for the codicil and confesses on Ansel's hidden recorder when confronted with the river photograph. Ansel gives the recording to Noor and Danny's mother before the sheriff, letting the family decide. The beat: catharsis and cost — justice delivered, but Ansel can no longer pretend the alphabetized world was ever clean.
